questions.text: Why should this lesson’s analyzer inspect the object header before interpreting parameter registers?

options.A: Every x86-64 object uses the same argument registers regardless of platform.
options.B: The format and machine select the ABI that gives register usage its meaning.
options.C: The header contains the complete original C signature of every function.
options.D: The optimization level alone determines all argument and return locations.

questions.explanation: For the fixtures, ELF x86-64 selects System V, COFF AMD64 selects Microsoft x64, and the Arm formats select their respective AAPCS64 variants. The ISA alone does not distinguish platform conventions.

questions.text: Under Microsoft x64, where do the four arguments of mixed(int i, double d, long long l, float f) arrive?

options.A: EDI, XMM0, RSI, XMM1, using independent integer and float lists.
options.B: RCX, XMM0, RDX, XMM1, using independent integer and float lists.
options.C: RCX, XMM1, R8, XMM3, using the argument positions as slots.
options.D: X0, D0, X1, S1, using the AAPCS64 integer and float counters.

questions.explanation: Microsoft x64 assigns the first four argument slots by position. Integer and floating-point registers share the positional index, unlike the independent System V lists.

questions.text: The analyzer computes an rsp-relative operand’s entry offset as displacement - depth. After three 8-byte pushes and sub rsp, 0x20, what entry offset does a load at [rsp + 0x60] have?
questions.explanation: The depth is 3*8 + 0x20 = 56 (0x38). Subtracting it from 0x60 gives entry offset 0x28 (40).
